title: Aspect: imperfective and perfective
objectives: I can explain what aspect expresses and choose an imperfective or a perfective verb in the past: a process, a repetition or a plain fact against one completed action with a result.
I can recognize the three ways aspect pairs are formed: a prefix, a change of suffix and a different stem.
I can explain why a perfective verb has no present, and use its present-looking forms to say what I will get done.
I can talk about tasks begun, finished and not yet done with 'почина́ти', 'закі́нчувати', 'вже', 'ще не' and 'наре́шті'.
I can explain how 'зроблю́', 'візьму́', 'почну́' and 'сказа́ти' are spelled and pronounced, and why 'вже' is sometimes written 'уже́'.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'роби́ти', made with the prefix 'з-'. It conjugates like 'роби́ти', with the same 'л' after 'б', but its present-looking forms mean the future: 'зроблю́', 'зро́биш', 'зро́блять'.

example.source: Have you made the salad yet?

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'писа́ти', made with the prefix 'на-'. Its forms follow 'писа́ти', with 'с' becoming 'ш': 'напишу́', 'напи́шеш', 'напи́шуть'.

example.source: Sam wrote a sentence in Ukrainian.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'чита́ти', made with the prefix 'про-'. It presents the reading as done, to the end of the text. Its forms follow 'чита́ти': 'прочита́ю', 'прочита́єш'.

example.source: Oksana has already read this book.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'купува́ти'. It is in the second conjugation, and its 'я' and 'вони́' forms add 'л' after 'п': 'куплю́', 'ку́пиш', 'ку́плять'.

The imperfective partner of 'да́ти'. In the present the '-ва-' drops, as in 'встава́ти', 'встаю́': 'даю́', 'дає́ш', 'даю́ть'. The 'вони́' form with no subject speaks of people in general, as English 'they' does in 'they give you a menu'.

example.source: Here they give you an English menu.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'дава́ти'. Its future is irregular and has to be learned: 'дам', 'даси́', 'дасть', 'дамо́', 'дасте́', 'даду́ть'. The past is regular: 'дав', 'дала́', 'дали́'.

example.target: Та́то дав гро́ші, і я купи́ла хліб.
example.source: Dad gave me money, and I bought bread.
example.source_literal: Dad gave money, and I bought bread.

vocabulary.note: The imperfective partner of 'взя́ти'. In the present an 'е' appears between 'б' and 'р': 'беру́', 'бере́ш', 'беру́ть'. In a café or a shop it is the usual verb for what you order or buy, where English says 'get' or 'have'.

example.target: Я завжди́ беру́ ка́ву з молоко́м.
example.source: I always get coffee with milk.
example.source_literal: I always take coffee with milk.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'бра́ти', on a different stem. Its future is 'візьму́', 'ві́зьмеш', 'ві́зьмуть', and its past is 'взяв', 'взяла́', 'взяли́'. After a word that ends in a consonant it is written 'узя́ти' ('Він узя́в ключ.'), by the euphony rule for 'у' and 'в'.
The imperfective partner of 'сказа́ти'. Its 'з' becomes 'ж' in every present form, as the 'с' of 'писа́ти' becomes 'ш', and the stress moves back after the 'я' form: 'кажу́', 'ка́жеш', 'ка́жуть'.

The perfective partner of 'каза́ти', made with the prefix 'з-', which is written 'с-' before 'к'. When 'говори́ти' means 'to say', 'сказа́ти' also serves as its perfective. Its future is 'скажу́', 'ска́жеш', 'ска́жуть'.

The imperfective partner of 'поча́ти'. It takes a noun in the accusative or an imperfective infinitive. When the thing itself begins and there is no object, the verb takes '-ся': 'Фільм почина́ється.', 'The film is starting.'

The perfective partner of 'почина́ти'. Its future has an 'н' that the infinitive does not show: 'почну́', 'почне́ш', 'почну́ть'. The past is 'поча́в', 'почала́', 'почали́', and with '-ся', for a thing that begins, 'почала́ся' ('Вечі́рка почала́ся.', 'The party began.').

example.source: Oksana has started reading a new book.

vocabulary.note: The imperfective partner of 'закі́нчити'. In the present '-ува-' becomes '-у-', and the stress stays on 'кі': 'закі́нчую', 'закі́нчуєш', 'закі́нчують'.

example.target: Зазвича́й я закі́нчую робо́ту о шо́стій.
example.source: I usually finish work at six.
example.source_literal: Usually I finish work at sixth.

vocabulary.note: The perfective partner of 'закі́нчувати', in the second conjugation: 'закі́нчу', 'закі́нчиш', 'закі́нчать'. With a school or a university as its object it means to graduate: 'закі́нчити університе́т'.

example.target: Мій брат закі́нчив шко́лу рік тому́.
example.source: My brother finished school a year ago.

vocabulary.note: One syllable, so it has no stress mark, and its 'в' before 'ж' is [w]. After a word that ends in a consonant, and at the start of a sentence, it is written 'уже́', a word of two syllables ('Він уже́ прочита́в.'). With a perfective verb it says that the result is there now.
It says that a long-awaited result has arrived, so it goes with a perfective verb. Said alone, 'Наре́шті!' means 'At last!'.

With 'не' and a perfective verb it means 'not yet': the result is expected but is not there. 'Ще ні.' is the short answer 'Not yet.' Without 'не' it means 'still' ('Я ще чита́ю.', 'I'm still reading.'), and before a noun 'another' or 'more' ('Я візьму́ ще я́блуко.', 'I'll take another apple.').

dialogues.title: Getting ready for the party
dialogues.context: On Friday evening Oksana and Taras go through the errands for a party at Oksana's home on Saturday. They say 'ти' to each other. A short answer repeats the verb alone ('Так, купи́в.'), the usual way to say 'Yes, I have.'

lines.target: Тара́се, ти вже купи́в хліб?
lines.source: Taras, have you bought the bread yet?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Так, купи́в. І сир тако́ж купи́в.
lines.source: Yes, I have. I bought the cheese too.
lines.source_literal: Yes, bought. And cheese also bought.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре. А ковбасу́?
lines.source: Good. And the sausage?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ще ні. Я її́ куплю́ за́втра на ри́нку.
lines.source: Not yet. I'll buy it tomorrow at the market.
lines.source_literal: Still no. I it will-buy tomorrow on market.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: А сала́т ти вже зроби́в?
lines.source: And have you made the salad yet?
lines.source_literal: And salad you already made?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Я поча́в його́ роби́ти, але́ ще не закі́нчив.
lines.source: I started making it, but I haven't finished yet.
lines.source_literal: I began it to-make, but still not finished.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: До́бре. А я вже зроби́ла борщ і купи́ла я́блука.
lines.source: All right. And I've already made the borscht and bought apples.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ти до́вго роби́ла борщ?
lines.source: Did it take you long to make the borscht?
lines.source_literal: You long made borscht?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, до́вго. Я почала́ о шо́стій, а закі́нчила о дев’я́тій.
lines.source: Yes, a long time. I started at six and finished at nine.
lines.source_literal: Yes, long. I began at sixth, and finished at ninth.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре. А сала́т я зроблю́ за́втра вра́нці.
lines.source: Very good. And I'll make the salad tomorrow morning.
lines.source_literal: Very well. And salad I will-make tomorrow in-morning.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, Тара́се!
lines.source: Thank you, Taras!
lines.source_literal: I-thank, Taras!

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Будь ла́ска! До за́втра!
lines.source: You're welcome! See you tomorrow!
lines.source_literal: Be kindness! Until tomorrow!

dialogues.title: A book, finally finished
dialogues.context: Before class, Sam tells his teacher Iryna Petrivna about the Ukrainian book she lent him. They say 'ви' to each other. Sam says 'весь ти́ждень', 'the whole week': 'весь' means 'all' or 'whole', and the phrase is in the accusative, which here says how long the reading went on. 'Щодня́' means 'every day'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день, Іри́но Петрі́вно!
lines.source: Good afternoon, Iryna Petrivna!
lines.source_literal: Good day, Iryna Petrivna!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: До́брий день, Се́ме! Ви чита́ли кни́гу?
lines.source: Good afternoon, Sam! Have you been reading the book?
lines.source_literal: Good day, Sam! You read book?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, я чита́в її́ весь ти́ждень, щодня́.
lines.source: Yes, I was reading it all week, every day.
lines.source_literal: Yes, I read it all week, every-day.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: І ви її́ вже прочита́ли?
lines.source: And have you finished it yet?
lines.source_literal: And you it already read?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так! Я наре́шті прочита́в її́ вчо́ра.
lines.source: Yes! I finally finished it yesterday.
lines.source_literal: Yes! I finally read it yesterday.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре! Вона́ ціка́ва?
lines.source: Very good! Is it interesting?
lines.source_literal: Very well! It interesting?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ду́же ціка́ва, але́ я чита́в ду́же пові́льно.
lines.source: Very interesting, but I read very slowly.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А нові́ слова́ ви написа́ли?
lines.source: And did you write down the new words?
lines.source_literal: And new words you wrote?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, написа́в. І я вже поча́в їх вивча́ти.
lines.source: Yes, I did. And I've already started learning them.
lines.source_literal: Yes, wrote. And I already began them to-study.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ду́же до́бре, Се́ме. А що ви бу́дете чита́ти по́тім?
lines.source: Very good, Sam. And what will you read next?
lines.source_literal: Very well, Sam. And what you will to-read then?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я ще не зна́ю. Мо́жна взя́ти ще кни́гу?
lines.source: I don't know yet. May I take another book?
lines.source_literal: I still not know. Possible to-take more book?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Звича́йно, мо́жна. Ось вона́.
lines.source: Of course you may. Here it is.
lines.source_literal: Of-course, possible. Here it.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Цю я прочита́ю шви́дко.
lines.source: Thank you! I'll read this one quickly.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! This I will-read quickly.

dialogues.title: Not coffee today
dialogues.context: In the morning Sam comes into Andrii's café. Andrii knows him well but says 'ви' to him, as to every customer, and Sam says 'ви' to Andrii. In 'як завжди́', 'as always', the word 'як' compares, as English 'as' does.

lines.source_literal: Good morning, Sam! Coffee with milk, how always?

lines.speaker: Сем

lines.source_literal: Good morning, Andrii! I always take coffee, but today will-take tea.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Чай? До́бре. А цу́кор?

lines.target: Ні, без цу́кру, будь ла́ска. Я вже пив ка́ву вдо́ма.

lines.source_literal: No, without sugar, be kindness. I already drank coffee at-home.

lines.target: А меню́ ви вже прочита́ли? У нас є нови́й сала́т.

lines.source_literal: And menu you already read? At us is new salad.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ще ні. А коли́ ви його́ зроби́ли?

lines.source_literal: Still no. And when you it made?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Сього́дні вра́нці. Він ду́же смачни́й.
lines.source: This morning. It's very tasty.
lines.source_literal: Today in-morning. It very tasty.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, я візьму́ сала́т і чай.
lines.source: All right, I'll have the salad and tea.
lines.source_literal: Good, I will-take salad and tea.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Ось ваш чай і сала́т. Смачно́го!
lines.source: Here are your tea and salad. Enjoy your meal!
lines.source_literal: Here your tea and salad. Of-tasty!

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Дя́кую! Сала́т ду́же смачни́й. Мо́жна раху́нок?
lines.source: Thank you! The salad is very tasty. May I have the bill?
lines.source_literal: I-thank! Salad very tasty. Possible bill?

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Звича́йно. Ось він. До за́втра, Се́ме!

lines.source_literal: Of-course. Here it. Until tomorrow, Sam!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: зроблю́, візьму́, почну́ and the other new verbs
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. Most of the new verbs are known verbs with a prefix, and a prefix does not change how the rest of the verb is spelled or said: 'зроблю́' keeps the 'л' of 'роблю́', and 'напишу́' keeps the 'ш' of 'пишу́'. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

The consonant changes of the present tense carry over to the perfective forms:

- After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф', the 'я' and 'вони́' forms of a second-conjugation verb add 'л': 'зроблю́', 'зро́блять'; 'куплю́', 'ку́плять'.
- In 'каза́ти' and 'сказа́ти' the 'з' becomes 'ж' in every form with a personal ending, as the 'с' of 'писа́ти' becomes 'ш': 'кажу́', 'ска́жеш'.
- 'Дава́ти' drops '-ва-' before a personal ending, as 'встава́ти' does: 'даю́', 'дає́ш'.
- 'Закі́нчувати' turns '-ува-' into '-у-', as 'купува́ти' does, but keeps the stress on 'кі': 'закі́нчую'.

Three verbs show a stem in their personal forms that the infinitive hides, and the stem is learned with the verb. In 'бра́ти' an 'е' appears between 'б' and 'р': 'беру́', 'бере́ш'. In 'поча́ти' an 'н' appears: 'почну́', 'почне́ш', and the imperfective 'почина́ти' shows the same 'н'. 'Взя́ти' has the stem 'візьм-': 'візьму́' [ʋizʲˈmu], 'ві́зьмеш'. Its soft sign marks the 'з' as soft before 'м', where no vowel letter could show it.

The prefix 'з-' is written 'с-' before 'к', 'п', 'т', 'ф' and 'х', and is said [s]: 'сказа́ти' is 'с-' plus 'каза́ти', while 'зроби́ти' keeps 'з-' before 'р'.

The letter 'в' before a consonant is [w], at the start of a word as well as at the end of a syllable: 'вже' [wʒɛ], 'взяв' [wzʲɑw]. Like the preposition 'в', many words that begin with this 'в' follow the euphony rule of the unit on stress. After a vowel they keep 'в' ('Я вже прочита́в.'); after a consonant, and at the start of a sentence, they take 'у'. So 'вже' becomes 'уже́', a word of two syllables with its own stress mark ('Він уже́ прочита́в.'), 'взяв' becomes 'узя́в', and 'вчо́ра' from the unit on the past becomes 'учо́ра' ('Що ти роби́в учо́ра?').

The letter 'щ' writes two sounds, [ʃt͡ʃ], as in 'ще' [ʃt͡ʃɛ] and 'щодня́', every day, a word made of 'що' and a form of 'день', with the 'н' soft before 'я'. The 'шт' of 'наре́шті' is two letters for [ʃt], and its 'т' is soft before 'і'. In 'весь', all, the soft sign makes the final 'с' soft. 'Гість', guest, in the culture note, has 'о' in its other forms, as in the plural 'го́сті': the closed syllable turns 'о' into 'і', as in 'кіт', 'кота́'.

Stress moves in several of these verbs, so learn it from the 'я' and 'ти' forms: 'зроблю́' but 'зро́биш'; 'куплю́' but 'ку́пиш'; 'скажу́' but 'ска́жеш'; 'візьму́' but 'ві́зьмеш'. In the past, the feminine of 'поча́ти', 'да́ти' and 'взя́ти' moves the stress to the ending: 'поча́в' but 'почала́'; 'дав' but 'дала́'; 'взяв' but 'взяла́'. The plural of 'сло́во' moves it the same way as 'мі́сто', 'міста́': 'слова́'.

rows: added after б, п, в, м, ф in the я and вони́ forms
for з in каза́ти and сказа́ти
the prefix з- before к, п, т, ф, х
before м in the stem візьм-
for в after a consonant or at the start
two letters, т soft before і

grammar.title: What aspect means: a process or one completed result
grammar.explanation:
Aspect, 'вид' in Ukrainian grammar, is the way a verb presents an action: as something going on, or as one whole that was completed. Nearly every Ukrainian verb has one aspect, and most actions are named by a pair of verbs: an imperfective verb, 'недоко́наний', literally 'not-completed', and a perfective verb, 'доко́наний', 'completed'. 'Чита́ти' and 'прочита́ти' both mean 'to read'; they differ in what they say about the reading.

English does part of this with other tools: 'I was reading' against 'I read it through', and 'I used to read' against 'I have read it'. Ukrainian has one past tense in everyday use, so the choice of verb does that work, and both verbs of a pair make their past with the endings of the previous unit: 'чита́в', 'чита́ла', 'чита́ли'; 'прочита́в', 'прочита́ла', 'прочита́ли'.

An imperfective verb names the action itself, without saying that it reached a result. It is used for three things:

- a process going on at the time: 'Я чита́в кни́гу.', 'I was reading a book.'
- a repeated or habitual action: 'Я ча́сто чита́в украї́нською.', 'I often read in Ukrainian.'
- a plain fact, when the question is only whether the action happened at all: 'Ти чита́ла цю кни́гу?', 'Have you read this book?'

A perfective verb presents one action as a completed whole, usually with a result that matters: 'Я прочита́в кни́гу.' means 'I read the book to the end' or 'I have finished the book'. A row of perfective verbs tells events one after another, each finished before the next begins: 'Я купи́в хліб і зроби́в сала́т.', 'I bought bread and made a salad.'

The same English past often translates either verb, so ask what the speaker presents: the activity, or its completion. 'Що ти роби́в учо́ра?' asks how someone spent yesterday; 'Що ти зроби́в учо́ра?' asks what they got done.

Some words point to one aspect, because their meaning fits only one of the two views:

- 'до́вго', 'ча́сто', 'завжди́' and 'щодня́', every day, describe duration or repetition, so the verb is imperfective: 'Сем до́вго писа́в.'
- 'наре́шті' says that an awaited result has arrived, so the verb is perfective: 'Сем наре́шті написа́в.'
- 'вже' usually comes with a perfective verb, for a result that is already there: 'Я вже купи́ла сир.' With an imperfective verb it says that the action took place at some time before: 'Я вже чита́в цю кни́гу.', 'I have read this book before.'
- 'ще не' with a perfective verb says that an expected result is not there yet: 'Я ще не прочита́в.', 'I haven't finished reading yet.'

examples.source: I was reading this book for a long time.

examples.target: Я купи́в хліб і зроби́в сала́т.
examples.source: I bought bread and made a salad.
Taras has finally finished his work.

grammar.title: Aspect pairs: a prefix, a suffix or another stem
grammar.explanation:
An aspect pair is two verbs with the same meaning that differ only in aspect. The partner of a verb cannot always be predicted, so each pair is learned as a pair, and from this unit on the course names the partner of every new verb. A verb is built from parts: the root, which carries the basic meaning; a prefix, a short part placed before the root; a suffix, a part between the root and the ending; and the ending itself. Pairs are formed in three ways.

The most common way is a prefix. The perfective is the imperfective with a prefix in front, and in these pairs the prefix adds no meaning of its own: it only makes the verb perfective. Which prefix a verb takes is learned with it:

- 'роби́ти', 'зроби́ти' (prefix 'з-')
- 'писа́ти', 'написа́ти' (prefix 'на-')
- 'чита́ти', 'прочита́ти' (prefix 'про-')
- 'каза́ти', 'сказа́ти' (prefix 'с-', the spelling of 'з-' before 'к')

The second way is a change of suffix. Here the imperfective is usually the longer verb:

- 'дава́ти', 'да́ти': the imperfective adds '-ва-'.
- 'купува́ти', 'купи́ти': '-ува-' against '-и-'.
- 'почина́ти', 'поча́ти': '-ина-' against '-а-'.
- 'закі́нчувати', 'закі́нчити': '-ува-' against '-и-'.

This gives a rough guide: in a prefix pair the perfective is longer, and in a suffix pair the imperfective is longer, often with '-ва-' or '-ува-'.

The third way is a pair on two different stems, which simply has to be memorized: 'бра́ти' and 'взя́ти', to take. 'Говори́ти' means 'to speak' or 'to say', and in the sense 'to say', 'сказа́ти' serves as its perfective. 'Що він говори́в?' asks 'What was he saying?', and 'Що він сказа́в?' asks 'What did he say?'.

Not every prefix makes a partner. Many prefixes add a meaning of their own and make a new verb. The prefix 'пере-' means 'again' or 'over': 'переписа́ти', literally 'over-write', means 'to rewrite', a new verb rather than the partner of 'писа́ти'. Later units teach these prefixes.

examples.target: Сем завжди́ купува́в ка́ву, а сього́дні купи́в чай.
examples.source: Sam always bought coffee, but today he bought tea.
What did you get done yesterday?

grammar.title: No present for the perfective, and verbs of beginning and finishing
grammar.explanation:
A present-tense verb describes an action going on now or happening regularly, and both are views of a process. A perfective verb cannot present an action as going on, so it has no present tense. It still has a set of forms with the present endings, but they mean the future, because the completed result is still to come. 'Я чита́ю.' is 'I am reading.'; 'Я прочита́ю.' is 'I will read it', to the end.

These future forms take the endings of the two conjugations from the unit on verbs, with the same consonant changes as the imperfective: 'прочита́ю', 'прочита́єш' like 'чита́ю'; 'зроблю́', 'зро́биш' like 'роблю́'. 'Да́ти' is irregular: 'дам', 'даси́', 'дасть', 'дамо́', 'дасте́', 'даду́ть'. The table gives four perfective verbs in full.

An imperfective verb makes its future with 'бу́ду' and the infinitive, as the unit on weather and plans showed: 'Я бу́ду чита́ти.', 'I will be reading.' 'Бу́ду' combines only with an imperfective infinitive; a perfective verb makes its future with its own endings. The next unit compares the futures in detail.

'Почина́ти', 'поча́ти', 'закі́нчувати' and 'закі́нчити' take a noun in the accusative ('Я почала́ робо́ту.') or an infinitive. The infinitive after them is always imperfective, because what begins or ends is a process:

- 'Я почала́ чита́ти.', 'I started reading.'
- 'Тара́с закі́нчив писа́ти.', 'Taras has finished writing.'

The verbs of beginning and finishing themselves come in both aspects and follow the rules of this unit: 'Я зазвича́й почина́ю працюва́ти о дев’я́тій.' for a habit, 'Сього́дні я почала́ працюва́ти о сьо́мій.' for one occasion.

examples.target: Я дам гро́ші, а ти ку́пиш сік.
examples.source: I'll give the money, and you'll buy the juice.
examples.source_literal: I will-give money, and you will-buy juice.

examples.target: Сього́дні я почала́ працюва́ти о сьо́мій.
examples.source: Today I started work at seven.
examples.source_literal: Today I began to-work at seventh.

culture.title: Hosting a party at home
culture.text:
Ukrainians often celebrate at home rather than in a restaurant: a birthday, a holiday or simply friends on a Saturday. A party at home means a full table, with several salads, a hot dish and something sweet, and the errands are shared out among family and friends, as Oksana and Taras share theirs. The guests are 'го́сті', and one guest is 'гість'. A guest brings something: a cake, fruit or flowers.

Some customs surprise visitors:

- Guests take off their shoes at the door, and the host often offers slippers.
- Flowers for a celebration come in an odd number: three, five or seven. Even numbers of flowers are brought to funerals.
- The host keeps offering more food, and 'Ще?' ('More?') is heard all evening. Leaving a little on the plate shows that you have had enough.
- A birthday is not celebrated before its date, and wishing someone a happy birthday early is thought to bring bad luck.
- At work, the person whose birthday it is usually brings a cake for colleagues.

When the last guest finally arrives and everyone sits down, the host may well say 'Наре́шті!', 'At last!'. The evening is long: people stay at the table and talk after the meal, and close friends often move to the kitchen to sit and talk.

paragraphs.target: У субо́ту вра́нці Тара́с купи́в ковбасу́ на ри́нку, а по́тім зроби́в сала́т. Окса́на до́вго приміря́ла су́кні. Наре́шті вона́ взяла́ зеле́ну.
paragraphs.source: On Saturday morning Taras bought sausage at the market and then made a salad. Oksana spent a long time trying on dresses. In the end she took the green one.
paragraphs.source_literal: In Saturday in-morning Taras bought sausage on market, and then made salad. Oksana long tried-on dresses. Finally she took green.

paragraphs.target: Вечі́рка почала́ся о сьо́мій. Оле́на до́вго співа́ла, а Андрі́й і Сем танцюва́ли. Сем їв борщ і сала́т. Борщ був ду́же смачни́й.
paragraphs.source: The party started at seven. Olena sang for a long time, while Andrii and Sam danced. Sam ate borscht and salad. The borscht was very tasty.
paragraphs.source_literal: Party began at seventh. Olena long sang, and Andrii and Sam danced. Sam ate borscht and salad. Borscht was very tasty.

paragraphs.target: Об одина́дцятій Окса́на сказа́ла: «Дя́кую! Свя́то було́ ду́же га́рне». Тара́с і Сем ще до́вго сиді́ли на ку́хні й говори́ли.
paragraphs.source: At eleven Oksana said: 'Thank you! It was a really lovely celebration.' Taras and Sam stayed on in the kitchen, talking for a long time.
paragraphs.source_literal: At eleventh Oksana said: 'I-thank! Celebration was very beautiful.' Taras and Sam still long sat on kitchen and talked.

questions.prompt: What did Taras do on Saturday morning?
choices: He bought sausage at the market and then made a salad.
questions.explanation: 'Тара́с купи́в ковбасу́ на ри́нку, а по́тім зроби́в сала́т.' Two perfective verbs tell two completed actions, one after the other.

questions.prompt: Why is 'приміря́ла' imperfective in 'Окса́на до́вго приміря́ла су́кні'?
choices: She tried on one dress and bought it.
The action is in the future.
The trying on went on for a long time, as 'до́вго' shows.
questions.explanation: 'До́вго' describes duration, so the verb presents the trying on as a process, not as one completed result.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows that Oksana made her choice?
questions.explanation: 'Наре́шті' and the perfective 'взяла́' present one completed result after a long wait.

questions.prompt: What did Taras and Sam do after Oksana thanked everyone?
choices: They sat in the kitchen and talked for a long time.
questions.explanation: 'Тара́с і Сем ще до́вго сиді́ли на ку́хні й говори́ли.' The imperfective verbs and 'до́вго' present the sitting and talking as an activity that went on.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its English meaning
Match each perfective form with its meaning
Which of these verbs is perfective?
exercises.explanation: 'Прочита́ти' is 'чита́ти' with the prefix 'про-', which makes it perfective. 'Купува́ти' is the imperfective partner of 'купи́ти'.

exercises.prompt: What is the perfective partner of 'бра́ти'?
exercises.explanation: 'Бра́ти' and 'взя́ти' are a pair on two different stems, so the partner has to be memorized.

choices: With a prefix on the perfective
With a change of suffix: the imperfective adds '-ва-'
exercises.explanation: In a suffix pair the imperfective is usually the longer verb. 'Дава́ти' adds '-ва-' to the stem of 'да́ти'.

exercises.hint_source: I have already made the salad.
exercises.explanation: The result is there now, so the verb is the perfective 'зроби́ти': 'зроби́в' for a man, 'зроби́ла' for a woman.

exercises.hint_source: Sam was reading the book for a long time.
exercises.explanation: 'До́вго' describes duration, so the verb is imperfective: 'чита́в'.
'Наре́шті' points to one awaited result, so the verb is the perfective 'купи́ти', in the feminine past.

exercises.hint_source: Tomorrow I'll buy the bread. Use 'купи́ти'.
exercises.explanation: The present-looking 'я' form of a perfective verb means the future. 'Купи́ти' adds 'л' after 'п': 'куплю́'.

exercises.hint_source: They will give the money tomorrow. Use 'да́ти'.
exercises.explanation: 'Да́ти' has an irregular future: 'дам', 'даси́', 'дасть', 'дамо́', 'дасте́', 'даду́ть'.

exercises.hint_source: Will you have coffee or tea? Use 'взя́ти'.
exercises.explanation: 'Взя́ти' has the future stem 'візьм-', and the stress moves back after the 'я' form: 'візьму́', 'ві́зьмеш'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says that the book was read to the end?
exercises.explanation: The perfective 'прочита́в' presents the reading as one completed whole. 'Я чита́в кни́гу.' names only the activity, and 'Я бу́ду чита́ти кни́гу.' is about the future.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Я прочита́ю кни́гу.' refer to the future?
choices: A perfective verb has no present, so its present-looking forms mean the future
The ending '-ю' always marks the future
exercises.explanation: A perfective verb presents a completed whole, which cannot be going on now. Its forms with present endings therefore mean that the result is still to come.
'Писа́в' is imperfective, and 'ча́сто' describes repetition, which the imperfective expresses. 'Наре́шті' asks for a perfective verb, and 'за́втра' does not fit a past verb.
What begins or ends is a process, so 'почина́ти', 'поча́ти', 'закі́нчувати' and 'закі́нчити' are followed by an imperfective infinitive: 'Я почала́ чита́ти.'

exercises.prompt: Why is 'сказа́ти' spelled with 'с' and not 'з'?
choices: The prefix 'з-' is written 'с-' before 'к', 'п', 'т', 'ф' and 'х'
The 'с' shows that the verb is imperfective
exercises.explanation: 'Сказа́ти' is the prefix 'з-' plus 'каза́ти'. Before 'к' the prefix is written 'с-' and said [s].

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'Він уже́ прочита́в.' but 'Я вже прочита́в.'?
choices: 'Уже́' is the form for 'він', and 'вже' the form for 'я'
After a word that ends in a consonant, 'вже' is written 'уже́' by the euphony rule for 'у' and 'в'
'Уже́' is used with perfective verbs and 'вже' with imperfective verbs
exercises.explanation: 'Він' ends in a consonant, so 'вже' becomes 'уже́'. After the vowel of 'я' it stays 'вже'.

exercises.prompt: In the café, Sam says 'Я завжди́ беру́ ка́ву, але́ сього́дні візьму́ чай.' Why does he use two different verbs?
choices: 'Беру́' is for coffee and 'візьму́' is for tea
'Беру́' is a habit, so it is the imperfective present; 'візьму́' is one choice still to come, so it is the perfective future
exercises.explanation: 'Бра́ти' and 'взя́ти' are an aspect pair. 'Завжди́' calls for the imperfective, and one completed choice today calls for the perfective, whose present-looking form means the future.

exercises.prompt: Sam tells Iryna Petrivna 'Я чита́в її́ весь ти́ждень.' and then 'Я наре́шті прочита́в її́ вчо́ра.' What does the change of verb show?
choices: The first sentence is about the reading as an activity, the second about finishing the book
The first sentence is about another book
Both sentences mean the same thing
exercises.explanation: The imperfective 'чита́в' with 'весь ти́ждень' presents a process; the perfective 'прочита́в' with 'наре́шті' presents its completed result.

exercises.prompt_source: I have already made the borscht.
Taras started reading a new book.
Tomorrow I will give the money.

exercises.hint_source: I have finally finished this book.

exercises.prompt_source: I have already bought the cheese.
exercises.explanation: The result is there now, so 'вже' goes with the perfective 'купи́ти'. At the start of a sentence 'вже' is written 'уже́'.

exercises.prompt_source: Taras was writing for a long time.
exercises.explanation: 'До́вго' describes duration, so the verb is the imperfective 'писа́ти'.
'Закі́нчити' is followed by an imperfective infinitive, because what ends is the process of reading.
In a café 'взя́ти' is the verb for ordering, and its 'я' form 'візьму́' means the future.
